guideTitle: Best Immersion Blenders for Frothing Milk (2026)
metaTitle: Best Immersion Blenders for Frothing Milk 2026
metaDescription: Stick blenders with milk frother heads compared: Mueller, MegaWise, MasterChef, Ganiza and Shardor kits sorted by whisk design, speed range and cleanup.
expertTake: The Mueller 800W 5-in-1 is the top pick for frothing milk, because twelve fixed speeds plus turbo let you run the frother head slowly for foam instead of spraying it. The MasterChef 3-in-1 is the value pick, since a frother head is the main point of its kit. Skip the whole idea if you only want a daily cappuccino, because a dedicated handheld whisk costs less and washes faster.
introParagraphs: Frothing milk with a stick blender works through the attachment, not the blade. A small coiled or caged head spins on the end of the stick and whips air into warm milk, so the quality of the result depends on speed control, head shape and the vessel you use.

That changes what matters when you shop. A big wattage figure does little for foam, and a stick with only one or two speeds tends to throw milk across the counter. This guide compares kits that include a frother head, and flags which controls and materials make a real difference to foam and to cleanup.

products.name: Mueller 800W 5-in-1 stick blender, 12 speeds with turbo
products.description:
The Mueller 800W 5-in-1 is the best frothing kit here because of its speed ladder. Twelve fixed speeds plus a turbo button let you hold the frother head at a low speed where milk folds air in gently, then step up for a quick finish. The kit includes a chopper, a whisk, a frother head and a 20 oz beaker.

That low end matters. A frother head whipped at full speed turns milk into spray before it becomes foam, and many two-speed sticks have no setting between idle and maximum. With twelve steps you can find the point where the head draws air without flinging it. The listing also leans on frozen fruit smoothies, which is a sign the motor has the torque to keep turning under load.

Use a tall jug with at least three times the volume of the milk, and keep the head just under the surface for the first few seconds. Rinse the frother head immediately, since milk protein dries into a hard film. The compromise is size: the kit has five tools to store, so it is overkill if foam is all you want.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a stick that froths well and still handles smoothies and soups.
pros: Twelve speeds let you run the frother slowly
800W motor with turbo for heavy tasks
20 oz beaker and chopper in the kit
Whisk head covers cream and eggs

products.name: MuellerLiving Ultra-Stick 500W 8-speed, with whisk and frother
products.description:
The Ultra-Stick is the slimmer, simpler version of the Mueller idea. A 500 watt motor, eight speeds and a turbo mode drive three attachments: a stainless blending shaft, a whisk and a milk frother. The body is slim enough for one-handed use and the listing highlights a non-slip grip.

For frothing milk, eight speeds is a useful middle ground. You get a few steps below the top where the frother head works gently, which is more than the two-speed kits offer. It will not match the twelve-step control of the 800W model, but it is lighter and cheaper to own.

Treat the frother as a small-batch tool. Fill the jug no more than a third with milk, warm the milk first and keep the head near the surface. Rinse the head and the shaft after use, and keep the attachments together in the drawer. It is a good compromise for coffee drinkers who also want a stick for soup.
products.bestFor: Coffee drinkers who want a slim stick with a frother and whisk.
pros: Whisk and frother in the box
cons: Fewer speed steps than the 800W model
Limited tools beyond the three attachments

products.name: MasterChef 3-in-1 stick blender with whisk and milk frother
products.description:
The MasterChef kit is built around the idea of a stick that blends, whisks and froths, and all three attachments are described as stainless steel. It is a licensed television-brand product, which makes it a plain, low-cost route to a frother head. The listing positions it as a 3-in-1 for whisking and frothing as much as blending.

Because the attachments are the point, the quality of the whisk and frother heads matters more than the motor. Stainless heads resist staining from coffee and do not hold milk odors the way plastic can. Expect fewer controls than the Mueller models, so you will pulse to keep the foam from splashing.

Cleanup is straightforward. Rinse the frother head right after use so milk does not dry, wipe the stick and store the three heads together. It sits in the lower price tier of this guide and suits anyone who wants a frother and a whisk without paying for a bigger kit.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the frother and whisk heads at the lowest outlay.
pros: Stainless steel heads resist coffee stains
Blend, whisk and froth in one kit

cons: Fewer speed steps for fine foam

products.name: MEGAWISE 3-in-1 stick blender, 12 speeds, whisk and frother
products.description:
The MEGAWISE states both numbers: a 400 watt rated motor and an 800 watt instantaneous peak. That honesty makes it easy to compare against sticks that quote only a peak. It includes twelve speeds with turbo and a three-piece kit of blending shaft, egg whisk and milk frother.

Twelve steps give it the same advantage for foam as the Mueller 800W, a slow setting where the frother draws air gently. The 400 watt rated motor is plenty for milk foam, which needs very little torque, and it makes the MEGAWISE a better choice than sticks with a bigger headline and fewer steps.

As with every frother, use a tall jug and warm milk. Rinse the head straight after use, since dried milk is stubborn. Check that the whisk and frother seat firmly before you start. It is a sensible pick for buyers who read specs and want the rated number stated.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a stated rated power and twelve speeds for foam.
pros: States both rated and peak power
Whisk and frother in the kit
cons: Smaller kit than the five-piece sets

products.name: Ganiza 6-in-1 corded stick blender with dual-rod frother
products.description:
The Ganiza stands out for its frother. A patented dual-rod frothing system drives two rods through the milk rather than a single coil, which the listing says froths milk quickly. It sits alongside a SUS 304 four-leaf blade, fifteen speeds and a six-piece kit.

Fifteen steps give a wide range for gentle foam. The 1100 watt figure is a peak-style claim, but milk needs little torque, so the motor is not the limit. What matters is the head: two rods create more turbulence and a finer foam than a single whisk in a quick run.

It is also the most expensive of the budget group by price tier. Rinse the rods immediately, since milk dries between them, and store the attachments in a bag. If foam is your main goal, this and the Mueller 800W are the two to compare.
products.bestFor: Foam-first buyers who like the idea of a dual-rod head.
cons: Upper price tier of the budget group
Headline wattage is a peak claim

products.name: SHARDOR 1100W stick blender with stepless variable speed

specList.label: Kit
specList.value: Shaft, 16 oz chopper, whisk and more

products.description:
The SHARDOR replaces numbered steps with a one-touch stepless speed control. That means there is no fixed step to find: you slide through the range until the frother draws air without splashing. The kit is a five-piece set with a stainless blending shaft, a 16 oz chopper and a whisk among the pieces.

Stepless control is the best match for foam. You can hold the head at exactly the speed that works for the jug and the milk, and adjust as the foam builds. The 1100 watt maximum is a ceiling, not an everyday figure, but the pure copper motor has more than enough for milk.

It is also the highest in price tier within the milk-frothing set. Rinse the attachments right after use and keep the control area dry, since milk splashes there. A good option for cooks who like fine, continuous control.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want continuous speed control for foam.
pros: Five-piece kit with chopper and whisk
cons: Highest price tier in the frother set

buyingCriteria.explanation: Milk foam needs a slow head. A two-speed stick jumps from idle to maximum and sprays milk, while the Mueller 800W offers twelve steps, the Ganiza fifteen and the SHARDOR a stepless range. Look for a stick that lets you work at a quarter of full speed. Test the idea at home with a manual wand if you are unsure, because the slow end of the range is where most of the foam is made.

The Ganiza uses a dual-rod frother, the MasterChef and Mueller Ultra-Stick use a single milk frother head. Rod count affects how much air is drawn in. All of them work best with warm milk in a tall jug.
Foam takes little torque, so the 400W rated MEGAWISE is as capable as the 1100W SHARDOR. Spend on control and head design instead. Power matters only if you also blend frozen fruit or thick soup.
Stainless frother and whisk heads, as on the MasterChef, resist coffee staining and do not hold odors. Plastic heads can retain milk smell. Check what the head is made of before you buy.
Milk protein dries to a stubborn film, so a rinse must happen at once. A kit with a snap-on head and a plain shaft is quick to wash. A five-piece set adds time.

Foam needs room. The Mueller 800W includes a 20 oz beaker, but a tall jug three times the milk volume works better. A narrow vessel keeps the head submerged and the foam contained. A glass jug also lets you watch the foam rise, so you can stop at the moment it doubles in volume.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed range for foam
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the steps available below full speed on each stick. The Mueller 800W, MEGAWISE and Ganiza offer 12 to 15 steps, the SHARDOR a stepless range. Foam quality depends on finding a slow setting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Head design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at single-coil, whisk and dual-rod heads and their materials. A stainless head resists staining and odors. The Ganiza dual-rod design is the most distinctive.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor reserve
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the rated and peak figures, from 400W rated on the MEGAWISE to 1100W max on the SHARDOR. Foam needs little power, so reserve matters only for smoothies and soups. Owner feedback patterns on milk foam informed this.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the pieces and the cleaning steps. Milk dries quickly on heads, so quick rinse access matters. A smaller kit is easier to keep clean. We also considered whether the heads snap on without tools, since a head that needs fiddling is one that gets skipped on a busy morning.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for foam
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six by relative price tier, from the MasterChef lowest to the SHARDOR highest. Each should offer a real advantage in control or head design.

faq.q: Can an immersion blender froth milk?
faq.a: Yes, with a frother or whisk head and warm milk in a tall jug. Run it at a low speed, since full speed throws milk out of the jug. Fill the jug to no more than a third, submerge the head a centimetre or two and let the foam build before lowering it into the milk.

faq.q: Do I need a powerful motor for foam?
faq.a: No. Foam takes little torque, so a 400W rated motor is enough. Control and head design matter more. A big motor only helps if you also plan to crush frozen fruit or puree thick soup with the same stick, in which case the Mueller 800W is the sensible pairing.

faq.q: Which is better, a stick kit or a handheld frother?
faq.a: A dedicated handheld frother is cheaper and quicker to wash. A stick kit makes sense if you also blend soup and smoothies. Many owners find the dedicated wand wins for a daily coffee, while the stick wins on the days that need soup, so the answer depends on how much of your use is foam.

faq.q: Why does my milk spray everywhere?
faq.a: The speed is too high or the jug too small. Use a tall jug, lower the speed and keep the head just below the surface. A head that breaks the surface sucks in large bubbles, which pop and leave a thin, watery layer instead of fine foam.

Yes, for cold foam. Warm milk gives a denser foam, while cold milk gives a lighter one. Whole milk froths best because fat and protein stabilise the bubbles, and plant milks vary, so try a barista-labelled carton if you use oat or soy.

faq.q: How do I clean the frother head?
faq.a: Rinse it in hot water right after use and brush the gaps. Dried milk is much harder to remove. Run the head in a cup of warm soapy water for a few seconds, then rinse and let it air dry before storing.
